title: The Seven Ravens
paragraphs: Once there was a man who had seven sons, and last of all a daughter. The little girl was very pretty, but she was so weak and tiny that they thought she would not live, and they said she should be baptized at once.

The father sent one of his sons running to the spring for water, and the other six ran along with him. Each of them wanted to be the first to fill his pitcher, and in their rush all seven dropped their pitchers into the well. There they stood, looking at one another like fools, with no idea what to do, because none of them dared go home. Meanwhile the father grew restless and couldn’t think what was keeping the boys so long. “Surely,” he said, “all seven of them have lost track of time over some game.” And when he had waited longer still and they hadn’t come, he flew into a rage and wished them all turned into ravens. He had barely finished speaking when he heard a croaking overhead. He looked up and saw seven coal-black ravens circling round and round. He was sorry to see his wish come true, but he didn’t know how to undo what was done, and so he consoled himself as best he could for the loss of his seven sons with his dear little daughter, who soon grew stronger and more beautiful every day.

For a long time she had no idea she ever had brothers, since her father and mother were careful never to mention them in front of her. But one day she happened to overhear some people talking about them. “Yes,” they said, “she is beautiful, all right, but it’s a shame her brothers were lost because of her.” This upset her terribly, and she went to her father and mother and asked whether she had any brothers and what had happened to them. They didn’t dare hide the truth from her any longer. They told her it had been the will of Heaven, and that her birth was only the innocent cause. But the little girl grieved over it every day and felt she had to do everything she could to bring her brothers back. She had no peace or rest until at last, one day, she slipped away and set out into the wide world to find her brothers, wherever they might be, and to set them free, whatever it cost her.

She took nothing with her except a little ring from her father and mother, a loaf of bread in case she got hungry, a little pitcher of water in case she got thirsty, and a little stool to sit on when she got tired. So she walked on and on until she reached the end of the world. She came to the sun, but the sun was far too hot and fiery, so she hurried off to the moon. The moon was cold and chilly, and it said, “I smell flesh and blood around here!” So she left in a hurry and came to the stars. The stars were friendly and kind to her, and each star sat on his own little stool. The morning star stood up and gave her a small piece of wood, saying, “Without this piece of wood you can’t unlock the castle on the glass mountain, and that is where your brothers live.” The little girl took the piece of wood, wrapped it up in a cloth, and went on until she reached the glass mountain and found the door locked. She felt for the piece of wood, but when she unwrapped the cloth it wasn’t there. She had lost the gift of the good stars. What was she to do? She wanted to save her brothers, and she had no key to the castle on the glass mountain. So this faithful little sister took a knife from her pocket and cut off her little finger, which was just the size of the piece of wood she had lost. She pushed it into the lock, and the door opened.

As she stepped inside, a little dwarf came up to her and asked, “What are you looking for?” “I’m looking for my brothers, the seven ravens,” she answered. The dwarf said, “My masters aren’t at home, but if you’d like to wait until they come back, please come in.” The little dwarf was just preparing their dinner. He brought their food on seven little plates and their drink in seven little glasses and set them on the table. Their sister ate a small bite from each little plate and drank a small sip from each little glass, but into the last glass she dropped the ring she had brought with her.

Suddenly there was a fluttering and croaking in the air, and the dwarf announced, “My masters are coming.” They came in hungry and thirsty and hunted for their little plates and glasses. One after another, they said,
“Who has eaten from my little plate? And who has been drinking from my little glass?”

“Caw! Caw! it seems to me
Human lips have been here, I see.”

When the seventh raven reached the bottom of his glass and found the ring there, he looked at it and recognized it as his father’s and mother’s. He said, “If only our little sister would come! Then we would be free.” The little girl had been standing behind the door the whole time, listening. When she heard this, she ran forward, and in an instant all the ravens took their true shape again. They hugged and kissed one another, and they all went happily home.
